chunks: My father narrated to us, may God be pleased with him, saying: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, linking it up through his chain to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said that the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said:

Two leaders who are not in power: The man who is following a corpse in a funeral procession does not have the power to return until the body is buried or permission is given to him, and a man who is on a Hajj pilgrimage with a woman does not have the power to depart until she completes her pilgrimage rites.

key_terms.يَنْفِرَ: To depart/move from a place (specifically for Hajj)

ai.seo_question: What are the two examples of 'leaders who are not in power' in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq uses this hadith to illustrate the concept of 'imarah' (leadership/authority) as a temporary, situational mandate rather than permanent political power, highlighting how social obligations create binding authority. The Prophet identifies the funeral follower and the Hajj companion as 'leaders' because they hold the right to delay the other's departure until the ritual is complete, a nuance that underscores the spiritual weight of communal duties in Shia jurisprudence.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 2-58 (The compiler of the book narrated) that his father - may God be pleased with him - narrated that Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar quoted Muhammad ibn Ahmad, who linked it up through a chain of narrators to Aba Abdullah as-Sadiq (MGB), who said that God’s Prophet (MGB) said,

“There are two leaders who are not in power: The man who is following a corpse in a funeral procession doesn’t have the power to return until the body is buried, and a man who is on a Hajj pilgrimage visit along with a woman doesn’t have the power to leave until she finishes her Hajj pilgrimage.”
